consensus_summary: Egypt conventionally symbolizes bondage to sin and the oppressive world-system from which God delivers his people, while also admitting a minority reading of Revelation 11:8 as apostate Jerusalem.
book_summary: Egypt specifically identifies Jerusalem as the covenant city in bondage under worldly rule and corrupted in its covenant role, especially in Revelation 11:8.
consensus_core_identification: The realm or condition of bondage under sin and the godless world-system.
book_core_identification: Jerusalem, the covenant city, considered as being in bondage and covenant corruption under worldly rule.
boundary_disagreement: The consensus applies the symbol broadly to sinful bondage and the world-system, whereas the book restricts it to a particular covenantal instance: apostate Jerusalem in bondage. It therefore excludes many generic devotional applications of “Egypt” and reclassifies Revelation 11:8 specifically as Jerusalem rather than the world in general.
material_contradiction: There is no contradiction at the level of bondage imagery: the book retains bondage under worldly power. The material difference is referential precision, replacing a generic domain or condition with one particular city embodying that condition.
rationale: The book preserves the consensus category of bondage under worldly power but narrows its extension to Jerusalem in covenant corruption. This is not novel because the consensus explicitly lists apostate Jerusalem as a recognized interpretation of Revelation 11:8, nor is it divergent because Jerusalem can function as a particular covenant community embodying the broader bondage category.
strongest_objection: The book may appear divergent because it identifies Egypt with Jerusalem rather than with sin or the world itself. Nevertheless, Revelation 11:8 directly calls the crucifixion city “Egypt,” Galatians 4:25 explicitly describes present Jerusalem as being in bondage, and the remaining citations develop Jerusalem’s corruption; this supports treating the shift as a contextual narrowing rather than replacement of the underlying bondage category.
